justification_text:
The point estimates for each horizon—1 day, 1 week, and 1 month—are all equal at 234.16 because this represents the most likely central value based on the available data and underlying trend at the time of the forecast. In probabilistic forecasting, such a consistent point estimate typically reflects an assumption that no major changes to the fundamental drivers of the variable (e.g., price, value, or another measure being forecasted) are expected in the near term. It may also indicate a reliance on historical data or recent performance to anchor the expectation, with the understanding that deviations around this value become more likely as the forecasting horizon extends.

The key driver behind the widening confidence intervals as the horizon increases is uncertainty. Over short timeframes like 1 day, there is less time for unexpected events or volatility to meaningfully impact the outcome, so the range (90% confidence interval) is relatively tight at [231.81, 236.51]. Over a week, more room exists for fluctuations, whether from market dynamics, human behavior, or other influencing factors, so uncertainty grows, reflected in a wider 1-week interval of [227.08, 241.24]. For the 1-month horizon, uncertainty compounds further as more external factors—macroeconomic shifts, geopolitical events, policy changes, or other shocks—become relevant, causing the most expanded confidence interval, [218.17, 250.15].

Certain risks or events could push outcomes outside the stated confidence intervals, particularly over the longer horizons. These could include unexpected, large-scale economic data releases, policy announcements, geopolitical crises, or extreme market sentiment shifts that were not reflected in the historical data used to inform this forecast. For instance, in the 1-month horizon, a major regulatory announcement or an economic shock could introduce extreme outcomes well beyond the bounds of the projected interval. It’s also worth noting that confidence intervals are probabilistic, meaning there is still a 10% chance that the actual outcome will be outside the interval even without unforeseen events—a feature inherent to this level of statistical confidence.
